paras: The lynching of the Tarno brothers was the reported hanging of three white men by a masked mob at Augusta, Arkansas, in the early hours of February 3, 1881, after they were jailed on a charge of attempting to assault a young white woman. Wire reports said the mob took the men from the jail, hanged them across the river and threw their bodies into the water, and the story ran in papers from Virginia to Dakota Territory. A later report said the prisoners were only whipped and released.

According to the Memphis Public Ledger, Miss Hamblett, daughter of a prominent Augusta merchant, was walking home from a neighbor's house shortly after dark, accompanied by a servant girl, when three men ordered her to halt. She ran, one of the men caught her arm near her father's gate, and the screams of the girl and the approach of a "colored man" drove them off, leaving her uninjured. The Omaha Bee's version of the wire instead said her clothes were torn from her person.

The accused were identified as three brothers named Tarno, recently from Missouri, and a Chicago Times special gave their names as Robert, Samuel and Jacob and said they had been drinking for two or three days. Other papers called them "three white men" and sons of wealthy Monroe County planters.

The men were caught soon after the attack, and the Little Rock wire said officers had to fight a crowd crying "Hang them!" and "Kill them!" to get them into the jail. At about one o'clock that night a company of masked men, given as about twenty, broke into the jail, bound and gagged the jailer and guards, and took out the prisoners. They carried them across the river and hanged them on trees on the opposite bank, then threw the bodies into the river.

The Chicago Times correspondent added that the mob crossed in boats to a grove of cottonwood and elm, held a "council" there, and that the men were said to have confessed and begged for mercy, though accounts differed. By this account the brothers resisted so hard that half a dozen men were needed to hold them, and they were bound, gagged with rags and hanged in the morning light before being dragged to the river.

No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage. The badly printed close of the Chicago Times special appears to say that no investigation or arrests were expected and that the Hamblett family was among the wealthiest in the state.

The first reports came from Little Rock on February 3 and 4 and were picked up by papers in Memphis, Lancaster, Alexandria, New Haven and Omaha, and through a New Orleans Democrat special in Savannah and Richmond. Weeklies in Minnesota, Ohio and Indiana reprinted short versions the following week under headings such as "A Prompt Lynching," and the Batesville Guard in Arkansas gave it a single sentence.

Headlines such as "Swift Retribution" and "Lynched for Attempt to Commit Rape" presented the hanging as punishment, and the wire called the accused "brutes" and "would-be rapists." The Memphis Public Ledger, which knew the young woman's family, wrote that "respectable people" in Arkansas would no longer wait on the courts but would "seek summary vengeance through the aid of Judge Lynch." The Chicago Times special, reprinted in Dakota Territory as "A Terrible Lynching," dwelt on the struggle and described the lynchers "yelling like demons," while the Savannah Morning News later headed its account "Served Them Right."

Every February report says the three men were hanged, though the Memphis Public Ledger thought it "hardly probable" that the bodies were thrown into the river. An unsourced item in the Savannah Morning News on March 10, whose details closely follow the Ledger's account, said instead that the prisoners were "soundly thrashed and turned loose." The papers also differ on the date, giving Tuesday night, the early hours of February 3, or the early hours of February 4, and on whether the family came from Monroe County or Missouri.

bases: Nearly all reports say a masked mob took three jailed men accused of an attempted rape from the Augusta jail and hanged them across the river (A1, A3, A7, A9), though one later report says they were whipped and released (A31).

A masked mob of about twenty broke into the jail and took out three prisoners accused of attempted rape, and most reports say it hanged them (A1, A3, A7, A30); a later Savannah item, whose details match the local account the Memphis Public Ledger cited, says the men were thrashed and turned loose (A31), so the deaths are contested.

Wire reports from Little Rock and a separate Chicago Times special agree the three were hanged (A1, A3, A6, A30), but a March report says they were thrashed and released (A31), and the Memphis Public Ledger doubted the bodies were thrown in the river (A9).

accounts.label: Little Rock wire report
accounts.gist: Three men attempted to rape Miss Hamblet, were jailed after officers fought a crowd, and at 1 a.m. a masked mob of about twenty gagged the guards, hanged the prisoners across the river and threw their bodies in the water.

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger, citing a Little Rock Gazette special from Augusta
accounts.gist: The Tarno brothers, recently from Missouri, chased Miss Hamblett on Tuesday evening but fled when a colored man approached; near midnight infuriated citizens took them across the river and put them to death, though the paper doubted the bodies went into the river.

accounts.label: Chicago Times Little Rock special
accounts.gist: Robert, Samuel and Jacob Tarno, drinking for days, were taken by boat to a grove, held a 'council' with the mob, resisted desperately, and were hanged at morning light and thrown into the river.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News item, March
accounts.gist: Three drunken men accosted Miss Hamblet and were jailed; that night unknown men overpowered the guard, carried the prisoners across the river, thrashed them and turned them loose.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Little Rock wire under headlines such as 'Lynched.', 'Lynch Law in Arkansas' and 'A Prompt Lynching', calling the accused 'brutes' and 'would-be rapists'.
The Memphis Public Ledger said Arkansas people would 'seek summary vengeance through the aid of Judge Lynch' rather than trust the courts.
The Chicago Times special, 'A Terrible Lynching', described the lynchers 'yelling like demons' while dwelling on the men's debauchery.
The Savannah Morning News headed its whipping version 'Served Them Right.'
